input: Download and learn a new chord progression app

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing whether the goal is to casually explore the app or deeply master it changes how comprehensive the learning plan needs to be.
Whether this is for solo practice, teaching others, or collaborating with bandmates affects which app features matter most.
The instrument the user plays (guitar, piano, etc.) determines which apps are most relevant and how chord progressions are visualized.
Budget (free vs. paid) and device type (iOS, Android, desktop) narrow down which apps are actually downloadable.
The user's current music theory level determines whether they need a beginner-friendly app or one with advanced harmonic tools.
Knowing what 'learned it' means — e.g., can play three new progressions, can compose a full song, can teach it — defines when the task is done.
How much time per day or per week the user can dedicate shapes the pace and structure of the learning plan.

gold.taskTitle: Download and learn a chord progression app
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to find, install, and get up to speed with a new app focused on chord progressions for music practice or composition.

questions.title: What instrument are you learning chord progressions for?
questions.description: Identifies the primary instrument (e.g., guitar, piano, ukulele) so the app recommendation is tailored to the correct chord layout and notation style.

questions.title: What is your current music theory knowledge level?
questions.description: Determines whether the user needs a beginner-friendly app with simple visuals or a more advanced tool with Roman numeral analysis and modal options.

questions.title: Are you willing to pay for an app, or free only?
questions.description: Establishes the budget constraint, which immediately filters out paid apps like Scaler 2 or keeps them in consideration.

questions.title: What device will you use — iOS, Android, or desktop?
questions.description: Determines which platform the app must be available on, since many chord progression apps are platform-specific.

questions.title: Is this for composing your own music or practicing existing songs?
questions.description: Clarifies the primary use case, which shifts the focus between compositional tools (e.g., chord generators) vs. learning/reference apps.

questions.title: Are you learning this solo or alongside bandmates or a teacher?
questions.description: Identifies whether collaboration or sharing features are needed, or if this is a purely personal practice tool.

questions.title: What does 'learned it' look like — a specific skill or outcome?
questions.description: Defines the success criteria so the plan has a clear endpoint, such as being able to write a full chord progression in a new key.
